_readme: schedule.json — the declarative job manifest for the merchandise-return engine's clock.
The engine is a set of modules that only produce value when something runs them while
nobody is watching. This file is that something's instruction sheet: it names every job,
when it runs, which engine modules it runs, which environment it needs, and what a human
should be told about the result.
scheduler.py reads this file and installs the jobs on whatever host it is running on
(cron, systemd timers, Windows Task Scheduler, or its own foreground loop).
WHY THIS FILE SHIPS AS *.json.example: the packager's file whitelist ships '*.json.example'.
It is a real, complete, working manifest, not a stub — scheduler.py loads it directly as the
built-in default. Copy it to 'schedule.json' (same directory, or your cwd, or point
$MER_SCHEDULE at it) only when you want to change something; your copy then wins.
NOTHING HOST-SPECIFIC LIVES HERE. No interpreter path, no scripts directory, no container
name, no log directory, no user identity. Those come from scheduler config (see 'config' in
scheduler.py --help). This file describes the WORK; config describes the MACHINE.

_schedule_note: EVERY 'schedule' BELOW IS UTC. This changed on 2026-07-28 and the reason matters.
The manifest used to say the expressions were 'host local time' and to write them as if
the host were on US Central: mer-engine was '0 8-17 * * 1-5', described as '08:00-17:00
Mon-Fri'. The host it actually runs on is a container whose local time IS UTC (`date` and
`date -u` agree). So the engine really ran 03:00-12:00 America/Chicago and was ASLEEP FOR
THE ENTIRE US BUSINESS AFTERNOON. Worst case, a vendor replying at 12:01pm CT on a Friday
was not processed until 03:00am CT on Monday — about 63 hours — while every tier deadline
in the ladder ran against that clock. A schedule and a description that disagree with
reality are worse than no schedule, because they stop anyone from looking.
WHY UTC AND NOT A TIMEZONE SETTING. Setting TZ per job would be the better fix — it is
DST-proof — but scheduler.py has no timezone concept: it hands the cron expression
verbatim to crontab/systemd/Task Scheduler, all of which interpret it in the host's local
zone, and a TZ in a job's `env` reaches only the CHILD PROCESS, never the moment the
clock fires. Rather than ship a `tz` field that silently does nothing, the expressions are
UTC — which is what the deployment host actually uses — and every 'schedule_human' below
states the real UTC time AND the CT time it lands on in both halves of the year.
DST. US Central is UTC-5 in summer (CDT) and UTC-6 in winter (CST), so a fixed UTC
expression drifts by one hour across the two changeovers. Every window below is therefore
widened by one hour so the intended Central business day is fully covered YEAR-ROUND; the
cost is one extra hour of coverage in one half of the year, which for jobs that read mail
and compute deadlines is free. The one job where the extra hour would matter — draining
the send queue — is bounded on both ends so it can never run outside daylight in either
offset. Single-instant daily jobs simply shift by an hour between summer and winter; that
is stated per job and is acceptable for quantities measured in days.
IF YOU RUN THIS ON A NON-UTC HOST, translate every expression below into your host's own
local zone, and fix 'schedule_human' at the same time. A description that no longer
matches its expression is the bug this note exists to prevent.
_log_note: log_max_lines was 500 and the hand-written wrappers used 400, which meant a traceback
from the every-minute hot path was rolled out of existence within the hour — the forensic
record of a bad night was gone before anyone woke up. It is 5000 here, and separately
every FAILURE is appended to an UNBOUNDED error log (heartbeat.py's `mer_errors.log`,
beside the heartbeat file) that nothing ever truncates. Bounded logs are for reading;
the error log is for evidence.
defaults._send_mode_note: MER_ENGINE_SEND IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THIS FILE. It is read from the host environment only -- the *_cron.sh wrappers export it from the operator's .env. When it is unset, mer_send.mode() returns 'off': every reply is still drafted and queued, and nothing is sent. A fresh install therefore cannot mail a vendor until a human turns sending on, which is the safe default. It lived here until 2026-07-29 with the value 'test', and because the operator's box needed 'live', somebody copied this manifest to schedule.json and edited it -- creating a second, untracked manifest that shadowed the real one and silently defeated three separate timezone fixes. Keeping host-specific values out of the manifest is what stops that recurring: see design rule 3 at the top of scheduler.py.

jobs.name: mer-stop-list-check
jobs.schedule_human: daily 13:05 UTC, right after the digest
jobs.description: Prints the do-not-contact register so a withdrawn instruction stays visible.
why_on_a_clock: M49. A user withdrew contact with a party mid-session; the instruction lived in a comment
and in one session's memory, and sessions are stateless. reserve_send() now refuses a
blocked recipient structurally, so the block is enforced whether or not anyone remembers.
This job exists so the register does not become invisible furniture. A stop nobody can see
is a stop somebody will eventually argue with, and a stale block silently prevents a send
that has since become legitimate. Printing it daily keeps it reviewable.
Read-only.

jobs.name: mer-digest
jobs.schedule_human: daily 20:05 UTC = 15:05 CT (CDT) — the 3PM audit the user asked for; 14:05 CT under CST, the unavoidable fixed-UTC DST drift
jobs.description: Cross-runtime status digest: every case, every unanswered reply, every send by ANY actor.
why_on_a_clock: M50. The board says what the state is. A local ledger says what THIS runtime did. Neither
answers the question that matters: what has happened on my cases, by anyone, and what is
waiting on me?
Three failures on one day were all this same blindness. Two vendor replies sat ~27 hours
unanswered and were found only because a session ran an ad-hoc mailbox search while working
an unrelated case. A session then reported a case as neglected when another runtime had
answered it inside 90 minutes. And a store manager received three copies of one letter,
because two runtimes each knew only their own sends.
So this reads the two sources every actor shares - the board and the MAILBOX - and reports
outbound from `in:sent`, not from a ledger. That is what makes another runtime's work
visible instead of looking like neglect.

READ-ONLY TOWARD EVERY COUNTERPARTY: it never writes to the board and never sends to a vendor, a regulator, or anyone involved in a case. The ONE exception is --email below, which mails the finished digest to the profile owner's own address and nowhere else, and therefore does reserve an idempotency entry. It used to say 'never sends, never touches the ledger' full stop; that stopped being true when --email was added and is corrected here rather than left to rot.
2026-07-30: moved to 15:05 UTC-5 and given --email. The user asked for one daily scan
at 3PM rather than an every-minute poller, on the grounds that vendors reply on
business timescales and the fast loop was producing noise rather than speed. He was
right: the every-minute path caught a reply in 60 seconds and drafted a WORSE letter
than a considered one, and two runtimes both awake is what put three copies of one
letter in a store manager's inbox.
--email matters as much as the schedule. A digest written to a log on a host nobody
reads is the same failure as the skip lines that hid an unwatched case for a day.

jobs.name: mer-engine
jobs.schedule_human: hourly at :00, 13:00-22:00 UTC Mon-Fri = 08:00-17:00 CT in summer (CDT), 07:00-16:00 CT in winter (CST)
jobs.description: The inbound->action loop: read new mail, classify, draft, then process the veto queue.
why_on_a_clock: This is the engine proper. Vendor mail arrives on the vendor's schedule, not the user's,
and every tier deadline in the ladder runs against the clock from the moment a reply lands.
Business hours only: a draft queued at 3am cannot be vetoed by a sleeping human, and the
veto window is the only thing standing between a machine-written letter and a real vendor.
THE HOUR RANGE IS UTC (see defaults._schedule_note). It was '8-17' with a comment that
called it business hours, on a host whose local time is UTC — so it ran 03:00-12:00 CT
and the engine slept through every US business afternoon. 13-22 UTC is EXACTLY the
intended 08:00-17:00 Central under CDT; under CST it lands an hour early (07:00-16:00
CT), which is the unavoidable one-hour DST drift of a fixed UTC expression. The winter
16:00-17:00 CT hour is not a hole in coverage: mer-hotpath watches the mailbox EVERY
MINUTE, 24/7, and dispatches this same engine the moment a reply lands. This hourly job
is the backstop behind that, not the primary detector.
env_notes: MER_ENGINE_SEND IS NOT SET HERE, on purpose -- see defaults._send_mode_note. It comes from the host environment (the *_cron.sh wrappers export it from the operator's .env). Unset means 'off': replies are still drafted and queued, and nothing leaves. Turning sending on is a deliberate act by a human on one box, not a value shipped to everyone.

MER_ENGINE_WINDOW_HOURS is the veto window: hours between a reply being drafted and it actually going out. It stays in the manifest because it is a behavioural default that is right for every install, not a property of one machine.
step_notes: The first step runs mer_engine via mer_hotpath --force rather than calling mer_engine.py
directly. --force runs exactly the same command, but takes the shared lock first, so this
hourly job and the every-minute mer-hotpath job can never classify the same reply at once.
That matters more than it looks: two concurrent runs produce two different LLM drafts, so
two different body fingerprints, and idempotency.reserve() would permit BOTH. The lock is
what makes the pair safe -- do not revert this step while mer-hotpath is scheduled.
send_queue.py --process ALSO runs here, but it is no longer the ONLY place it runs; see
the mer-send-queue job below. It used to be, and that turned the veto window into a lie:
a letter drafted at 11:50am CT with a 3-hour window was 'due' at 2:50pm CT and did not
actually leave until the next drain -- which, with the broken schedule above, was 03:00am
the following Monday. 61 hours late, still quoting a deadline computed on Friday. Keeping
the step here as well is deliberate redundancy: if the frequent drain job is ever removed,
the queue still drains rather than silently filling up forever.

jobs.name: mer-send-queue
jobs.schedule_human: every 10 minutes, 13:00-22:59 UTC daily = 08:00-17:59 CT in summer (CDT), 07:00-16:59 CT in winter (CST)
jobs.description: Drain the veto queue: send every queued letter whose veto window has actually expired.
why_on_a_clock: THE VETO WINDOW MUST MEAN WHAT IT SAYS. A queued letter carries a promise -- 'this goes
out in 3 hours unless you cancel it' -- and that promise is only kept if something looks
at the queue shortly after those 3 hours are up. Until now the only drain was bolted to
the hourly mer-engine job, so the real send time was 'the next business-hours engine run',
which over a weekend was up to 61 hours after the letter was due. A letter that arrives
two days late still quoting the deadline it was written against is worse than no letter:
it tells the vendor the deadline is not real.
WHY IT IS STILL BOUNDED TO DAYLIGHT. The other half of the original design was sound: a
draft queued at 3am cannot be vetoed by a sleeping human, so nothing may LEAVE the
machine overnight. This job therefore runs frequently but only inside 13:00-22:59 UTC,
which is daytime in Central under BOTH DST offsets. The hot path still queues 24/7 and
still cannot drain (mer_hotpath refuses structurally, see FORBIDDEN_DISPATCH); an
overnight draft simply waits for the morning, which is what a human would expect.
IT RUNS SEVEN DAYS A WEEK ON PURPOSE. A letter queued Friday afternoon with a 3-hour
window is due Friday evening; draining only Mon-Fri would hold it until Monday morning
and reintroduce the exact delay this job exists to remove. Saturday morning delivery of
an escalation letter is normal and harmless; a 61-hour delay is not.
env_notes: This job does not decide WHETHER to send -- it drains letters whose veto window has already closed. It inherits send mode from the host environment exactly as mer-engine does, so the two cannot disagree: there is no longer a manifest value for them to disagree about.
step_notes: The heartbeat step proves THE JOB RAN, not that the drain succeeded -- the scheduler runs
every step regardless of the previous step's exit code, so this beat is a liveness signal
only. Whether the drain itself worked is carried by the first step's own exit code, which
the 'alert' stdout mode below escalates via fail_rc_above.

stdout.footer: (the veto window on each of these had already expired)
stdout.fail_message: send_queue --process exited {rc} - the veto queue did not drain, so approved letters are sitting unsent while their deadlines run.

jobs.name: mer-hotpath
jobs.description: Event-driven hot path: watch the mailbox cursor and fire the engine the moment a reply lands.
why_on_a_clock: The hourly engine job means a vendor reply can sit unnoticed for an hour, and from Friday
evening to Monday morning for roughly sixty. Every tier deadline in the ladder is already
running by then. This job costs one Gmail API call a minute while the mailbox is quiet and
does nothing else; when the cursor moves and a message was genuinely added to the inbox, it
dispatches the SAME mer_engine.py the hourly job runs. It is a trigger, not a second engine.
It runs 24/7 on purpose and is still safe overnight, because it never drains the send queue:
send_queue.py --process stays on the business-hours mer-engine job, so a draft queued at 3am
cannot go out before a human is awake to veto it.
env_notes: This dispatches the same module as mer-engine and therefore obeys the same host MER_ENGINE_SEND. It is structurally forbidden from draining the send queue (FORBIDDEN_DISPATCH in mer_hotpath.py): it detects and dispatches, it never sends.
step_notes: mer_hotpath writes its own heartbeat on every tick -- idle, dispatching, or crashing --
so no separate beat step is needed here. A failed dispatch also REWINDS the mailbox
cursor, so the mail that triggered the failure is retried on the next tick instead of
being skipped forever.

jobs.name: mer-heartbeat
jobs.description: The watchdog's watchdog: compare every component's last heartbeat to its own cadence and alert on a missed beat, a failure, or a non-zero exit.
why_on_a_clock: Every other job in this manifest is SILENT WHEN HEALTHY, which is the right design for
output and a catastrophic one for liveness: it makes 'nothing is wrong' and 'nothing is
running' produce identical evidence. This engine has failed that way at least four times
(2026-07-18, 07-20, 07-26, 07-28). The canonical shape is an expired credential: every
per-case query throws, the exception handler prints one line and continues, and the run
finishes by printing 'done. 0 HIGH item(s)' -- which is exactly what a quiet week prints,
while deadlines pass on every open case.
So liveness gets its own channel. Every scheduled component writes {name, ts, ok, err} on
EVERY tick, success and failure alike, into one heartbeat file; this job is the only
thing that READS that file, and it speaks up on three conditions and no others: a beat
that did not arrive when it was due, a beat that says ok:false, and a non-zero exit code.
A component that is broken can no longer report itself green, because the write that
reports green is the same write that would have carried the error.
Ten minutes is chosen against the fastest cadence being watched (the one-minute hot path,
which is allowed to miss five minutes before it counts as missing) and against the
slowest useful human response. Alerts de-duplicate per component per condition with an
hour of cooldown, so a component broken overnight wakes you a few times, not 144.
Components that only run in business hours declare an active window in their own beat,
and this checker ignores them outside it -- otherwise it would report the engine missing
every night and be muted within a week.
env_notes: The Telegram bot token is read from the shared secrets file by the alerter itself and is
deliberately not listed as a job variable; WHO gets alerted comes from the profile.

stdout.footer: (component health; the alert itself has already been pushed)
stdout.fail_message: heartbeat --check exited {rc} - THE HEALTH CHECKER ITSELF IS BROKEN. Nothing is watching the engine until this is fixed.

jobs.name: mer-case-tick
jobs.schedule_human: daily at 14:00 UTC = 09:00 CT in summer (CDT), 08:00 CT in winter (CST)
jobs.description: The daily case tick: walk every open case, compute what is due, surface only what needs a human.
why_on_a_clock: Deadlines pass whether or not any mail arrives. The tick is the only job that fires on the
mere passage of time, so it is what keeps a silent case from quietly aging out. Once a day
is the right sampling rate for quantities measured in days.
step_notes: The heartbeat step proves the daily tick RAN. Without it, a case-tick that silently stopped
firing would be indistinguishable from a week in which no case needed action -- both produce
no output at all, which is this manifest's definition of healthy.

jobs.name: mer-coverage-audit
jobs.schedule_human: daily 14:15 UTC = 09:15 CT (CDT), just after mer-case-tick
jobs.description: Fails if ANY live case has no derivable Gmail watch scope.
why_on_a_clock: M47. case_queries already refuses to guess a query it cannot derive safely, and logs
each skip. Logging is not telling. A case has gone dark from the moment it was created
- no MAIL FROM block, no CONTACTS address - and nobody learned of it for a day. Every
other case had a query; the newest one did not, and demand letters went out on it into
a mailbox with nothing watching for the reply.
new_case.py now writes a MAIL FROM block at creation, which stops NEW cases going dark.
This job is the backstop for the other ways it happens: a description edited on the
board, a vendor that starts replying from a domain nobody listed, a case imported by
hand, or a guessed domain that was simply wrong. It exits NON-ZERO, so an unwatched
case becomes a failing job - the one signal that reliably escalates - instead of a line
in a log file.
Read-only: it resolves queries and prints. It never writes to the board, never sends.

jobs.name: mer-drift-gate
jobs.schedule_human: daily 14:20 UTC = 09:20 CT (CDT), after the coverage audit
jobs.description: Fails if any deployed skill tree diverges from the master, or holds a secret.
operator_only_why: drift_gate.py compares deployed trees against the MASTER, so it only means anything on
the machine that holds the master — its own NOT_SHIPPED list excludes it from the
package. But this manifest ships verbatim, so every recipient was registering a clock
line for a module they do not have: a job that fails every time it fires, and a red
scheduler --selftest on an otherwise correct install. Reported 2026-07-31 from a
recipient's box. scheduler.py skips a flagged job only when its module is genuinely
absent; here, where drift_gate.py exists, it runs exactly as before.
why_on_a_clock: M51. SKILL.md sec 7 has always said: edit the master only, never a copy, because divergence
between copies is the original sin that split this skill's two predecessors apart. It
happened again anyway and nobody knew. One deployed tree was four milestones stale AND
carried two modules that existed nowhere else - one of which promoted cases to auto-send
with no veto window, the other of which called the raw mail transport directly, bypassing
the send token, the mailbox guard and the do-not-contact register. Neither had been
reviewed, because neither was ever in the master to review.
It was found by running a diff by hand while checking something unrelated - the same way
the three preceding incidents were found. A rule that depends on somebody thinking to look
is not enforcement.
It also checks for credentials in a distributable tree: a live OAuth refresh token was
found inside the engine folder of a skill whose documented model is 'hand the folder to
anyone'. Read-only; it reports and exits non-zero, it never copies or deletes.

jobs.name: mer-recall-sweep
jobs.schedule_human: daily 14:25 UTC = 09:25 CT (CDT), after the coverage audit and drift gate
jobs.description: Fails if any product case has not had its recall check run.
why_on_a_clock: M54. The recall check is the most valuable single lever in the ladder and the one nobody
thinks to pull. The first time it was actually run it found a CPSC recall with an exact model
match on a $3,000 chair, whose mandated remedy included a FULL REFUND - on a case that had
already been through Tier 1 and Tier 2 with nobody looking.
It also found the reason it matters most: a recall remedy is keyed to MODEL AND SERIAL, not to
proof of purchase. That is the exact wall a lost-receipt case hits, and two live cases were
stuck against it.
M53 made recall_check a blocking lever in the remedy map, which meant it was satisfied by
somebody CHOOSING to run it. This project's whole lesson register is a list of things that
were supposed to happen because a document said so. So it goes on the clock and exits
non-zero: an unchecked product case becomes a failing job rather than a good intention.
Service cases (a subscription, a membership, a bank fee) are exempt and say so - there is no
manufactured article to recall, and a gate that fires where it cannot apply is a gate people
mute. Read-only; it reports and never writes.

jobs.name: mer-calendar-sync
jobs.schedule_human: daily at 14:30 UTC = 09:30 CT in summer (CDT), 08:30 CT in winter (CST)
jobs.description: Mirror each open case's phase deadline onto its due date, then upsert one all-day calendar event per dated case.
why_on_a_clock: Two steps, in order, because the calendar reads the due date the first step writes.
This is the only job that always speaks: it prints a one-line summary every run so the
clock itself is auditable. Everything else here is silent-when-healthy, and a set of jobs
that are all silent gives you no way to tell 'nothing wrong' from 'nothing running'.

jobs.name: mer-delivery-check
jobs.description: Post-send bounce sweep. Read-only: reads the send ledger and the mailbox, sends nothing.
why_on_a_clock: Sending reports success the moment the mail server accepts the message for relay. A message
can be accepted and bounce minutes later, and nothing in the engine ever looks back — so a
dead escalation looks alive while its deadline clock keeps running. Three passes a day means
a bounce surfaces within about four working hours; the overnight sends are caught at 08:00.
Do not raise the frequency without lowering DELIVERY_CHECK_LOOKBACK_HOURS, or you will just
re-report the same bounce more often.

stdout.fail_message: delivery_check exited {rc} with no output - the bounce sweep did not complete.

jobs.name: mer-sol-watchdog
jobs.schedule_human: Mondays at 15:00 UTC = 10:00 CT in summer (CDT), 09:00 CT in winter (CST)
jobs.description: Statute-of-limitations sweep. Read-only: reads the board and prints, writes nothing.
why_on_a_clock: Every other deadline in the engine is our own. The statute of limitations is the OUTER clock,
and nothing in the loop watches it: a case can be perfectly on schedule against every internal
deadline and still cross the date after which no suit — and so no credible threat of suit — is
possible. The limitations period moves exactly seven days per week, so a daily check would
produce six identical answers and one useful one. Weekly is the correct sampling rate.
Monday morning puts it at the start of a week with time left to act.

stdout.footer: (record-only observation; nothing was written to the board)
stdout.fail_message: sol_watchdog exited {rc} with no output - the SoL sweep did not complete.

jobs.name: mer-unmatched-review
jobs.schedule_human: Mondays at 15:30 UTC = 10:30 CT in summer (CDT), 09:30 CT in winter (CST)
jobs.description: Weekly missed-mail sweep: return-related inbound that matched no live case query. Read-only.
why_on_a_clock: The engine matches inbound to a case by a per-case mailbox query. That is precise but narrow,
and mail it does not match is mail the engine never sees at all — so no event inside the loop
can ever trigger a review of it. Only a sweep over the whole inbox can. This is a slow leak,
not an emergency, and a week's accumulation is small enough to read in one sitting, which is
what makes it get read. The window is 8 days against a 7-day cadence: the extra day is
deliberate overlap so a late or skipped run cannot open a hole.
The 30-minute offset from the SoL sweep keeps two mailbox jobs off the same minute.

stdout.footer: (read-only observation; no case was opened and no mail was answered)
stdout.fail_message: unmatched_review exited {rc} with no output - the missed-mail sweep did not complete.
